Remission means the reduction, lessening, or cancellation of something that is harmful, burdensome, or negative — a disease, a punishment, a sin, or a debt. Think of it as something pressing down on you that suddenly eases up or lifts entirely.

The word is used across several different fields, and the meaning shifts slightly depending on context. But the unifying thread is always the same: something unwanted has been reduced or removed, at least for now.
1. Medical Remission — The Most Common Use Today

This is the use you'll encounter most often in modern life. When a serious illness — most commonly cancer, but also conditions like multiple sclerosis or lupus — goes into remission, it means the signs and symptoms of the disease have significantly decreased or disappeared.

This is a crucial point: remission is not the same as being cured. A cure means the disease is gone forever and will never return. Remission means it has retreated — the body is no longer showing active signs of the disease — but it could potentially come back. Doctors treat remission as very good news, but they continue to monitor the patient carefully because of that possibility.

There are two important types of medical remission:

Complete remission (also called full remission) means no detectable trace of the disease remains. Tests, scans, and blood work all come back clear. The disease is essentially invisible — but again, "invisible" doesn't necessarily mean "gone forever."

Partial remission means the disease has reduced significantly — for instance, a tumour has shrunk dramatically — but has not disappeared entirely. It's a step in the right direction, but the disease is still present to some degree.

When a disease that was in remission returns and becomes active again, that is called a relapse — the opposite of remission.

"After months of chemotherapy, her doctor told her the cancer was in complete remission — there were no signs of it anywhere in her body."
2. Remission of Sins — The Religious Use

In religious contexts, especially in Christianity, the phrase "remission of sins" means the forgiveness or wiping away of sins. The idea is that sins — like a debt — are officially cancelled or erased, usually through confession, faith, baptism, or divine grace. The sin is no longer held against the person; it has been "remitted."

"The sacrament was performed for the remission of sins."
3. Remission of a Sentence — The Legal Use

In law and criminal justice, remission refers to the reduction or cancellation of a punishment, almost always a prison sentence. If a prisoner is granted remission, their sentence is shortened — they are released earlier than originally ordered.

This typically happens as a reward for good behaviour in prison, or it can be granted by a government through a general amnesty (a mass pardon issued for a group of people).

Note the distinction from a pardon: a pardon forgives the offence itself and can wipe the conviction off the record. Remission simply reduces the length of the punishment — the conviction still stands, but the person serves less time.

"He had been sentenced to eight years, but was granted two years' remission for good conduct and was released early."
4. Remission of a Debt or Penalty — The Financial Use

In finance or governance, remission means the official cancellation or reduction of a financial obligation — a debt, a fine, a tax, or a penalty. When an authority "remits" a debt, they are letting the person off the hook, either partially or fully.

"The government announced a remission of late-filing penalties for small businesses that had struggled during the economic crisis."

More broadly — and less commonly — remission can describe a temporary easing in the force or intensity of anything, not just illness or punishment. This usage is somewhat literary or formal.

"During a brief remission of the blizzard, they made a run for the car."
The Unifying Thread Across All Uses

No matter the context, remission always follows this pattern:

Something negative or oppressive — a disease, a sin, a punishment, a debt, or even a storm — was present and active. Then, through some process (treatment, forgiveness, a legal decision, or simply time), it has been reduced, eased, or removed — either temporarily or permanently.

The word carries a sense of relief, but often also a sense of caution — particularly in medicine and law, because remission can be reversed. It is not the final, permanent victory. It is a reprieve.
How Remission Differs from Similar Words

Remission vs. Cure: A cure is final and permanent — the disease is gone and will not return. Remission is the retreat of the disease, which may or may not last. Every cured patient went through remission; not every patient in remission is cured.

Remission vs. Pardon: A pardon cancels both the punishment and the guilt of an offence — it's a full legal forgiveness. Remission only reduces the punishment (usually the sentence served). The conviction itself remains.

Remission vs. Relief: Relief is a general, everyday word for when something painful eases. Remission is the formal, precise term used in medical, legal, religious, and official contexts. You feel relief; a doctor diagnoses remission.

In short: wherever you see the word "remission," ask yourself — what is the thing being reduced or lifted? Answer that, and you have understood the word completely in its context.
